The Common bulbul (Pycnonotus barbatus) is a widespread passerine inhabiting diverse habitats across sub-Saharan Africa, and its life-history traits have been quantified through both field observations and captive studies. At a body temperature typical of active passerines (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the species exhibits a basal metabolic rate (BMR) of 86 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 86 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value aligns closely with predictions from allometric equations for birds of this size class and reflects the moderately high metabolic demands of a generalist frugivore that forages actively throughout the day. The maintenance of such an elevated resting metabolism is likely linked to the species' relatively small body mass and its need for sustained activity within a sometimes unpredictable tropical environment. Comparative data suggest that the BMR of Pycnonotus barbatus is intermediate between that of more sedentary congeners and those occupying cooler highland zones, where thermoregulatory costs are higher. The measurement was obtained under thermoneutral conditions during the inactive phase of the daily cycle, ensuring that the recorded value represents a genuine basal state.

Reproductive parameters in Pycnonotus barbatus have been documented from nest monitoring programs and museum egg collections. Clutch size typically ranges from 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt], and females generally produce approximately 2.5 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 clutches each year], a reproductive schedule that yields an annual output of roughly five to eight offspring per breeding pair. This pattern corresponds to a maximum reproductive rate that is consistent with the moderate fecundity expected for a medium-sized passerine of the Afrotropics, where extended breeding seasons permit repeated nesting. The timing of these events appears to be cued by rainfall patterns, with peak laying activity coinciding with periods of high fruit and insect abundance, thereby ensuring adequate provisioning for nestlings. Data from a consistent temperature regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during the active metabolic phase confirm that such thermal conditions do not impose a constraint on the species' ability to sustain this reproductive effort.

Egg dimensions, critical for understanding maternal investment and hatchling condition, have been characterized from measurements of closely related taxa. Based on length and width ranges of 20.3 to 22.1 millimeters and 14.6 to 15.2 millimeters respectively, the calculated initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is 3.44 grams [Ww0 = 3.44 grams]. This egg mass represents a substantial investment relative to adult female body mass, a pattern common among passerines that incubate for extended periods. The shelled eggs are typically pale with reddish speckling, a cryptic coloration that may reduce predation risk in open cup nests. The energetically costly process of egg formation and incubation places significant demands on the female, who must balance thermoregulatory needs with foraging time. Hatchling mass is closely tied to initial egg mass, and variations in the latter can influence chick survival during the critical first days after emergence, when the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental brooding and feeding.

Developmental milestones from hatching to independence have been estimated from a combination of captive rearing data and field observations of related species within the Pycnonotidae. The incubation period, based on data from the closely related Eurillas curvirostris, lasts approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] at an incubation temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Following hatching, the altricial nestling develops rapidly, and fledging—the point at which the young bird first achieves sustained flight—occurs at 11.5 days after hatching [tx = 11.5 days after hatching] under the warmer thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This brief nestling period is typical for small-bodied passerines and reflects the high predation pressures that favor rapid development and early departure from the nest. Even after fledging, the young remain dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks as they refine their foraging skills and learn to identify edible fruits and insects, a period of post-fledging care that gradually shifts them toward nutritional independence.

The species exhibits a moderate pace of life with respect to maturation and longevity. Sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 49.5 days after hatching [tp = 49.5 days after hatching] when maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a relatively early age compared to larger passerines. However, the time since birth at first brood, when a female successfully produces her first clutch, is deferred until approximately 401.5 days after hatching [tR = approximately 401.5 days after hatching] under those same thermal conditions (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), indicating a delay between the acquisition of reproductive competence and the initiation of breeding. This lag likely allows young birds to establish territories, accumulate fat reserves, and gain experience before committing to the energetic demands of reproduction. Maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], again at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value that is somewhat greater than that of many similar-sized open-nesting passerines and suggests that the species may experience relatively low adult mortality in its preferred wooded savanna and garden habitats. Adult body mass shows modest sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an ultimate wet weight of 33.3 grams [Wwi = 33.3 grams] and males reaching a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 36.8 grams [Wwi = 36.8 grams].
